Fireside talk shapes The Chimney-Corner, Stowe's book of essays and sketches from 1866. She gathers readers near the hearth to mull over children, neighbors, and housekeeping. Grief and faith enter the talk as well, in a plain and friendly voice.

Many pieces were written during and just after the Civil War. They carry a mother's seasoned wisdom and a tired nation's mood. Small moral dramas of daily life matter more here than grand events. For readers who loved the warmth of her novels, the book feels like Stowe thinking aloud, close and unhurried, with no need to preach.
swinburne-poems-ballads-1866:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published Poems and Ballads in 1866, a year after Atalanta in Calydon made his name. The new book scandalized Victorian England. Reviewers attacked its passion and paganism so fiercely that the first publisher withdrew it, and another quickly took it up.

Dolores, a hymn to a cruel goddess of pain, leads the notorious pieces. The Garden of Proserpine imagines death as peaceful sleep beyond love and weariness. Other poems praise Sappho, freedom, and the sea in rushing, musical lines. Swinburne's technique dazzled even his enemies. The volume, complete in its first series here, made him the wild star of late Victorian poetry.
the-book-of-quinte-essence-or-the-fifth-: The Book of Quinte Essence, 1866. The fifth essence. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth-pg1366: Charles Reade's 1861 historical novel about the parents of Erasmus: a young Dutchman torn between love and the church in the 15th century. Richly researched and passionately told, it brings medieval Europe to life. A great Victorian historical novel, too little read today.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume sixteen of Casanova's memoirs: the wanderer wanders on. Europe's courts and prisons. A life without pause. Sixteenth volume: courts and prisons, the wanderer never rests, Europe's courts and prisons, courts and prisons of Europe.
the-path-of-the-king-pg1966: John Buchan's 1921 episodic novel tracing the path of the king: from a Viking wanderer to Abraham Lincoln. The idea of leadership through the ages, told with his narrative gift. An unusual and fascinating Buchan. Buchan's kings are leaders in every age.
thoreau-yankee-in-canada-1866:
Henry David Thoreau's A Yankee in Canada saw print in 1866, after his death, a posthumous collection. The volume joins the Canada travel tale with his Anti-Slavery and Reform Papers in one last book. Slavery in Massachusetts, Life Without Principle, and Wendell Phillips stand among its fierce reform pieces in print.

Thoreau toured Quebec in 1850 and found old French Canada quaint, priest-ridden, and unfree in its own way. The travelogue mixes soldier lore, cathedral visits, and St. Lawrence scenery with his Yankee skeptic's dry wit throughout. Slavery in Massachusetts, his angriest speech, damns his state for returning fugitives under federal law in 1854. Life Without Principle scorns the money chase and calls work a form of prayer when freely chosen. The set shows Thoreau the reformer beside Thoreau the walker, one pen, two fires.
tob-0166:
Bahá'u'lláh, founder of the Bahá'í Faith, wrote The Seven Valleys in Baghdad around 1860, in answer to a Sufi correspondent's questions. In luminous Persian prose, it maps the soul's journey to God through seven valleys: search, love, knowledge, unity, contentment, wonderment, and finally true poverty and absolute nothingness. A companion piece, The Four Valleys, accompanies it.

Each valley has its perils and its signposts, described through parable, poetry, and quotation from earlier mystics. The Seven Valleys is the Bahá'í faith's most beloved spiritual text, read devotionally far beyond its original Sufi setting. English readers meet Persian mysticism at its most concentrated, in a short book meant for a lifetime.
tob-10066:
Christian D. Ginsburg, a Christian scholar of Hebrew, wrote an early English study of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition connected with the Zohar. His subject had few reliable guides in English when he wrote. He set out to explain its doctrines, trace its development, and survey its literature.

Readers learn what Kabbalah teaches about God and creation, how its ideas grew through the Middle Ages, and which books and teachers matter most. V1 evidence notes the study served for decades as the main English guide to a difficult subject. It remains useful as both an introduction and a record of nineteenth-century scholarship.
tob-10266:
Eliphas Levi, whose real name was Alphonse Louis Constant, published Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie in French in 1854. He wrote the work in two parts, doctrine first and ritual second. Most later occult writers drew on it, knowingly or not.

Levi ties magic to the tarot, the Kabbalah, and a force he calls the astral light, which trained will can direct. He gives rules, symbols, and rites for high magic while warning against fraud and black magic. Read in the original French, the book shows the style that made Levi the father of modern occultism.
tob-10466:
Volume two of Calvin's Institutes carries his system forward from Christ the Redeemer through the work of the Holy Spirit to the church and its sacraments. Where the first volume founded the doctrine of God and Scripture, this one asks how salvation reaches actual people. Prayer, providence, and the Christian life receive extended treatment.

Calvin explains the church's ministry, baptism, and the Lord's Supper, and closes with civil government and the hope of resurrection. His famous teachings stand in argued form, not slogans. Together the two volumes form Protestantism's most influential theological work, still read by students tracing how Reformed belief was built.
tob-12966:
James Legge, the Scottish missionary and scholar, spent decades translating China's classic books. His Chinese Classics series gives the Chinese text, an English translation, long notes, and full introductions for each work. The volume described by its evidence covers the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, two short Confucian treatises.

The Great Learning traces a path from ordering one's own thoughts to governing a state in peace. The Doctrine of the Mean praises balance, sincerity, and holding to the middle way. Legge's notes explain hard passages line by line. His series set the standard for all later English work on Confucian texts.
tob-4066:
Max Muller devoted much of his life to the Rig-Veda, the oldest religious text of India. His Rig-Veda-Sanhita presents the collection of 1,028 Sanskrit hymns with the learning of the age's leading orientalist. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the work anchored Western study of the Veda.

Fire god Agni, storm god Indra, and Ushas the dawn receive hymn after hymn of praise, prayer, and myth. Sacrifices, battles, weddings, and riddles all enter the songs. Muller's edition, with its vast labor of editing and translation, made the hymns a subject scholars everywhere could share. The book remains a monument of Victorian Oriental scholarship.
tob-4166:
Andrew Lang, the Scottish folklorist and man of letters, published Myth, Ritual, and Religion in 1887 as his manifesto in the science of religion. Lang opposed Max Muller's school, which read all myth as a disease of language about the sun. He argued from custom instead.

Lang holds that the savage rites and beliefs of living peoples explain the strange, irrational parts of Greek and other myths: the myths are fossils of ritual ages. He ranges over totemism, sacrifice, and the making of gods. The book is the anthropological school's classic statement, complete, and a model of learned argument written with a storyteller's ease.
ufo-hearings-house-1966:
Congress called the Air Force to account on UFOs in the spring of 1966. The House Committee on Armed Services held its hearing on April 5, with the public and press at full attention. A wave of sightings over Michigan that March had forced the issue.

The astronomer Allen Hynek, the Air Force's own adviser, told the panel the subject deserved true science at last. Generals laid out the Blue Book files and held that most cases had plain causes. The hearing pushed the Air Force to seek an outside study. From that push came the Condon study and the end of Blue Book.
un-ga-res-a-69-66:
Half the world has already banned nuclear arms from its soil, and Resolution A/69/66, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks that fact. Any group of states may make a pact to keep such arms out of its lands in full. That right stands in the 1968 pact against the spread of nuclear arms. Five zone pacts are named with praise, from Latin America to Africa and the Pacific.

With the Antarctic Treaty, those pacts have freed the whole southern half of the world, and the seas beside it, from nuclear arms. Mongolia's own lone-state free status is recalled as well. Till such arms end for good, the text holds, zones of this kind are a firm step toward that end.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 69/66 at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It decides to convene the Third Conference of States Parties and Signatories to Treaties that Establish Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones and Mongolia. The one-day conference is set for New York in 2015. Its purpose is to examine ways of strengthening cooperation among the zones and with Mongolia. The treaties' parties recognize Mongolia's single-state nuclear-weapon-free status alongside their own arrangements.
un-sc-res-1366:
Action on preventing armed conflict came with Resolution 1366, adopted on 30 August 2001. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a full report on prevention. Its lessons drew on failed efforts before the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre. Small arms flows kept making wars worse and longer.

The Council vows to treat prevention as a core part of its work. It will watch danger spots closely and act early, with missions to tense regions where states agree. The Secretary-General should flag threats, rights abuses, and disputes that could turn violent. Peacekeeping mandates may add disarmament work and police for the peace that follows. Regional bodies, above all in Africa, need more capacity and funds.
un-sc-res-1466:
UNMEE was extended as demarcation approached on 14 March 2003. Prisoners of war had been freed and sent home by both sides. Crossings of the Temporary Security Zone's southern edge caused concern. The Boundary Commission's ruling of 13 April 2002 awaited marking on the ground. The peace process was about to enter its decisive phase, the Council noted.

The Council extended UNMEE to 15 September 2003, at the troop and observer levels set by resolution 1320 (2000). Both parties were urged to meet their Algiers duties and to work with the Red Cross on the questions left open. They had to work fully and swiftly with UNMEE and give it complete freedom of movement. Every limit on the mission had to go at once. The Council backed UNMEE's power to check the parties' conduct inside the zone. Mine action work by the mission was also praised.
un-sc-res-1566:
Terrorism's definition and reach were pressed forward on 8 October 2004. Beslan and other attacks had swollen the count of victims, children among them. The Council restated resolutions 1267 (1999), 1373 (2001), and 1540 (2004). It reminded states that every counter-terrorism step had to honor human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law. Its three counter-terrorism bodies were told to work more closely together.

The Council condemned all acts of terrorism in the strongest terms, whatever their motive, wherever and by whomsoever committed. It recalled that crimes meant to kill or maim civilians, or to take hostages in order to terrorize a public, can never be justified. States were called to join every anti-terrorism convention as a matter of urgency. They had to speed agreement on the draft comprehensive convention on terrorism. A working group was set up to weigh practical measures against groups and persons outside the Al-Qaida sanctions list.
un-sc-res-166:
Security Council Resolution 166, adopted on October 25, 1961, recommended Mongolia for membership in the United Nations. Mongolia had sought a seat since 1946, but Cold War bargaining kept its bid blocked for fifteen years. A package deal that year, which also cleared Mauritania, at last let the landlocked Asian state through the council.

The General Assembly admitted Mongolia two days later. The text follows the standard form for new members: the council finds the applicant peace-loving and able to carry out the Charter, then passes the choice to the Assembly. For Mongolia, the vote ended a long wait at the door of world politics.
un-sc-res-1666: Security Council Resolution 1666, issued in 2006, comes to the collection through the official record held by English Wikisource. Fifteen votes stand behind the text, five of them belonging to permanent members with veto power. The decision those votes produced is preserved whole here, ready to be read against the debates that surrounded it.
un-sc-res-1866: Resolution 1866, from 2009, is a formal Security Council decision preserved in official-record form via English Wikisource. Its number is its citation, the handle by which diplomats and scholars refer to it. The entry behind that handle is complete: findings, decisions, and the reporting duties that usually send the matter back for review.
un-sc-res-1966:
War crimes courts need an ending plan, and Resolution 1966, adopted in December 2010, created one. The tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda were finishing their trials. The Council set up a residual mechanism to carry on their leftover duties for years afterward.

The new body tracks fugitives, protects witnesses, guards the archives, and can retry or refer cases as needed. It has branches in Arusha and The Hague, matching the two courts it serves. The text matters because justice for mass crimes does not end with the last big trial, and someone must keep the record.
un-sc-res-266: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 266 is catalogued here under 1969. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-366:
Namibia's occupier was given a deadline to declare itself on 17 December 1974. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a Council for Namibia. The World Court's 1971 opinion held that South Africa must withdraw. Pretoria still refused and ruled the territory by force. Its repression of Namibians and its racial laws drew the Council's anger.

The Council condemned the continued illegal occupation of Namibia. It condemned the racial and repressive laws South Africa applied there. South Africa had to make a solemn declaration that it would obey the United Nations decisions and the Court's opinion. It then had to take the steps needed to withdraw and hand power to the Namibian people. The Council would meet on or before 30 May 1975 to review South Africa's compliance and weigh the next steps.
un-sc-res-66:
Fighting broke out again in south Palestine in December 1948. The acting mediator sent word of the new clashes, which began on 22 December. On 29 December 1948 the Council called for a fast ceasefire. The governments had to use resolution 61 without more delay. That text told forces to pull back to their October lines. The mediator's orders under it also had to be obeyed.

United Nations observers needed full freedom to watch the truce on the ground. The Council wanted the truce checked in full. Its call came as talks on Rhodes were about to open. Those talks led to the 1949 truce deals. This text helped push the sides toward them.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Preventing wars before they start is the theme of Resolution 1366, adopted unanimously on 30 August 2001. The Council had before it the Secretary-General's report on the prevention of armed conflict, with ten principles and proposals for a system-wide strategy. It recalled the failures that preceded the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre, and the threat from illicit small arms flows.

The Council declares conflict prevention an integral part of its core duty. It stresses that primary responsibility rests with national governments, with the UN in support. It promises prompt attention to early warnings from the Secretary-General under Article 99, more Council missions to tension areas, and preventive deployment with host consent. It backs fact-finding missions, regional prevention strategies, and stronger prevention capacity in bodies such as the OAU and ECOWAS. Peacekeeping mandates should include disarmament and child-soldier rehabilitation where fitting.

Resolution 1466, adopted on 14 March 2003, keeps the Ethiopia-Eritrea peace process moving toward marking the border. The Boundary Commission had issued its ruling on the line in April 2002, and both sides had accepted it as final. Prisoners of war had been sent home, and the UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, was in place as the marking phase drew near.

The Council extends UNMEE until 15 September 2003. It urges both countries to work with the Boundary Commission, follow its marking directions, and give its field staff safety on the ground. It voices worry about crossings into the Temporary Security Zone and new anti-tank mines there. It also demands full freedom of movement for UNMEE and notes drought and hunger pressing on both countries.

On 8 October 2004 the Council passed Resolution 1566 by a full vote. It hones the Council's words on terror. All states must fight terror by all means the Charter and world law allow, it says once more. It voices deep alarm at the growth in the slain, children among them. Hate and zealotry drive more and more of the attacks, in land after land. States were told to work in full with the Council's three anti-terror teams. Those teams, in turn, must work as one.

The text reached past the known foes as well. A team was set up to draft real bars, such as bans on trips and frozen funds, for terror-linked men and groups past Al-Qaida and the Taliban. Law binds this fight too, the Council stressed.

Mongolia's road to the UN took sixteen years of Cold War bargaining. The landlocked state had applied repeatedly since 1946. Great-power vetoes blocked it each time. A package deal finally cleared the way in 1961. Resolution 166 was adopted on 25 October 1961 by nine votes to none. The United States abstained.

The Council recommended the Mongolian People's Republic for admission. The Assembly seated Mongolia two days later. Mauritania entered in the same bargain. Washington disliked recognizing a Soviet ally. It let the vote pass anyway, swallowing its doubts. This resolution thus marks a rare Cold War compromise: two locked doors opened together, widening the UN toward true universality.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 31 March 2006, and the terms for settling the Abkhazia conflict are restated. The work of the Secretary-General's Special Representative, helped by Russia as facilitator and by the Group of Friends, is backed. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force together kept the conflict zone stable.

Any settlement, the Council insists, must come by peaceful means within Georgia's recognized borders. Both sides are called on to finish a package of documents on non-use of force and refugee return without delay. Georgia is urged to take Abkhaz security concerns seriously, and the Abkhaz leadership to face the need for a dignified return of displaced people and respect for their rights.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended on 23 July 2007. The group had been renewed in stages since 2003, most recently that February alongside the authorization of the African Union mission. The embargo's carve-out for supplies meant only to build Somalia's security sector is recalled in detail.

The group's mandate is extended for a further period so it can keep gathering evidence of embargo violations and report through the sanctions committee. Somalia's transitional institutions, it is stressed, must keep working toward effective national governance. The renewal kept independent eyes on arms flows into Somalia at a moment when a new regional force was deploying and the security picture was shifting fast.

Georgia's United Nations mission is extended on 13 February 2009, after the August 2008 war. A six-point agreement of 12 August 2008 and follow-up measures of 8 September had set the ceasefire terms. Geneva discussions between the sides had begun in October, and the Secretary-General's February report proposed a revised security regime for the conflict zones.

The August and September arrangements are recalled, and respect for the 1994 Moscow ceasefire's separation-of-forces rules is called for until a new security regime is agreed. Avoiding force and any ethnic discrimination is stressed, and free humanitarian access is demanded. The mission's mandate is extended for a new period, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on how the parties are carrying out the resolution.

The war crimes courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda were both winding down in 2010. On 22 December that year the Council adopted Resolution 1966. It created a new body, the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. Some work would still remain after the two courts closed. Fugitive trials, appeals, and witness protection all needed a home.

The Mechanism was designed as a small, temporary body with two branches. The Rwanda branch would start work on 1 July 2012. The Yugoslavia branch would start on 1 July 2013. From those dates, the Mechanism would take over the courts' remaining duties and legal powers. The Council told both courts to finish all their remaining work by the end of 2014. They also had to prepare a smooth handover of files and tasks.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was still needed in 1969, even though the island had grown calmer. The Secretary-General reported that recent improvements had held. Cyprus agreed that the force should stay beyond 15 June 1969. Resolution 266 was adopted unanimously on 10 June 1969.

The Council reaffirmed its earlier Cyprus resolutions. It urged the parties to act with the utmost restraint and to make good use of the calmer climate. The force's stay was extended for a further period ending on 15 December 1969. The Council expected that enough progress toward a final solution would be made by then. Such progress might allow the force to withdraw, or at least to be cut down.

Resolution 366, adopted unanimously on 17 December 1974, condemns South Africa's grip on Namibia in the bluntest terms yet. The Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a UN council for the territory; the World Court ruled in 1971 that South Africa was obliged to withdraw. Pretoria answered with continued occupation, brutal repression of Namibians, and moves to break the territory's unity through ethnic homelands.

The Council condemned the illegal occupation and the persistent refusal to obey the Assembly, the Council, and the court's opinion. It condemned the repression and human rights violations as well. It demanded that South Africa withdraw its administration and stop carving up the territory, steps toward the free Namibia the UN had promised since the 1960s.

Fresh war broke out in south Palestine days before 1949. Shots had rung out on 22 December 1948. The stand-in mediator sent word of the clash. Resolution 66 passed on 29 December 1948 by eight votes to none. Three states held back, the two Soviet bloc teams and the United States among them.

Both sides had to call an instant halt to the guns. Old truce terms from November had to be put in force. UN men had to watch the truce in full, with free range. A Council team would meet at Lake Success on 7 January 1949. It would weigh how far each side had obeyed. Cuba and Norway would join the team from New Year. The new peace talks body, set up that month, was urged to start work fast.

Food for civilians sat inside the sanctions on Iraq in 1990, with one gate left open for cases of real need. The embargo of Resolution 661 covered food, except in humanitarian circumstances. Several member states had written to the sanctions committee about the food situation in Iraq and Kuwait. Resolution 666 set out how that need would be judged.

The Council decided that its sanctions committee would keep the food situation under constant review. Aid agencies had to report urgently on conditions. Children under fifteen, expectant mothers, the sick, and the elderly needed special attention. If the committee found an urgent humanitarian need, it would report to the Council at once. Food could then be supplied through the United Nations, working with the Red Cross or other aid bodies. The text also noted that medical supplies were not covered by the embargo.
walsh-examination-dorchester-1566:
John Walsh of Dorchester was called before a church court officer in 1566 to answer claims of sorcery. The Examination of John Walsh preserves that rare early session in print. Most later witch cases went to crown courts, but Walsh faced church discipline instead.

Question by question, the record shows how a lone man said to work magic was handled. The officers probe his books, his charms, and the help he gave his neighbors. No gallows waits at the end of this story, and that sets it apart. The pamphlet catches the years before the great witch panic took hold.
westcott-gospel-resurrection-1866:
Brooke Foss Westcott, the Cambridge scholar who later became bishop of Durham, published The Gospel of the Resurrection in 1866. The book began as essays on the meaning of Easter for faith and life. Westcott treats the resurrection not as one doctrine among many but as the center.

He argues that the risen life of Christ reshapes how believers read history, nature, and their own deaths. His method joins close Greek study to wide meditation on the church's worship across the ages. Victorian readers found in Westcott a learning that prayed, and the book shaped Cambridge theology for decades.
whittier-snow-bound-1866:
John Greenleaf Whittier published Snow-Bound in 1866, just after the Civil War, and it made him financially secure at last. Whittier set the long poem in his boyhood home in Haverhill, Massachusetts, remembering a great snowstorm that sealed the farmhouse for days. He dedicated it to the family circle it describes, most of them by then dead.

As the storm rises, the family gathers at the hearth: father, mother, uncle, aunt, brother, sisters, a schoolmaster boarder, and a storytelling guest. Each portrait is drawn with tender exactness, and the firelight holds off the cold and the reader's knowledge of loss. Whittier called it a winter idyll. It became the great American fireside poem and his most perfect work.
windsor-castle-pg2866: William Harrison Ainsworth's 1843 Windsor Castle: Henry VIII and Herne the Hunter. The great historical romance of old England. Tudor splendor and ghostly legend. Herne the Hunter haunts Tudor Windsor, ainsworth's pageant, Ainsworth's Tudor pageant and legend.
